🤝 Iraq reaches deal with Kataib Hezbollah — without the US
Iraq’s government has reached a last-minute agreement with Kataib Hezbollah instead of forcing the militia out of a key town south of Baghdad it has controlled since 2014, according to Al Jazeera.
🔴 Officials had accused the group of stealing hundreds of millions in state oil.
🔴 Facing threats of armed resistance and intervention by Iran’s Quds Force commander, Baghdad opted for a compromise rather than a confrontation.
🔴 The deal establishes a shared security presence starting tomorrow afternoon, mixing army, police, and militia fighters under a new command.
Iraqi government didn't get a total military victory—the militia keeps its role. But Iraq proved a much larger point: it is capable of managing its own complex web of factions and security challenges through internal consensus and regional diplomacy, without US interference.

events.text:
🤖 Anduril founder promotes AI-driven autonomous weapons to target ‘Russian tanks’
Palmer Luckey, founder of defense-tech startup Anduril, has recently advocated the use of autonomous weapons, arguing that a system capable of distinguishing a "Russian tank" from a school bus full of children is preferable to a "dumb mine."
In response, Walter Isaacson, who interviewed Luckey, pointed to current US policy requiring human oversight of drone strikes. Luckey countered by saying that this is not a permanent moral principle and [could be changed](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/77636).
Beyond the inflammatory framing – Russia is not at war with the United States – Luckey’s argument overlooks several serious [problems](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76660) that critics have repeatedly raised:
🔴 AI can get targets wrong. The [destruction of a school in Minab](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75462), Iran, killing children, has highlighted the risks of flawed targeting, outdated intelligence and over-reliance on automated systems
🔴 Can Anduril actually control its autonomous systems? Reports of AI agents escaping test environments and [breaching other companies’ digital infrastructure](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/77995) raise questions about whether Anduril and other defense-tech firms can reliably control increasingly autonomous AI models and robotic systems
🔴 Who is legally responsible? If an autonomous weapon kills the wrong target, who bears responsibility? With a conventional mine, accountability can be traced to those who planted it. Autonomous systems make that chain of responsibility far less clear
🔴 How does AI identify a tank’s nationality? Weapons platforms are often shared across countries, and national insignia can be obscured by mud or removed altogether. The challenge becomes even greater when forces use captured equipment – as the Houthis have done with Saudi weapons, or Russian forces with NATO-made equipment captured in Ukraine.

🇮🇷 New footage shows US-Israeli attack on Iran’s petrochemical hub
Several plants in southern Iran shut down or cut production after April 6 strikes disrupted shared electricity, water, and oxygen supplies. Newly released footage published by Fars News shows the attack on Jam Petrochemical, one of the facilities hit in Asaluyeh.
👉 Asaluyeh is home to Iran’s largest concentration of gas processing and petrochemical plants. It accounted for about 75% of the country’s methanol production capacity at the time, according to industry data provider ICIS. Methanol is one of Iran’s major chemical exports. After strikes on Asaluyeh and another hub in Mahshahr, Iran suspended petrochemical exports in April to prevent shortages at home.
More than seven months later, work is still underway at Jam. The company said this week that debris removal and preparations to rebuild its damaged butadiene unit were ahead of schedule.

events.title: Telegram
events.text:
🇸🇦 Saudi wealth fund headquarters damaged in Riyadh missile attack
Windows were blown out across several floors of Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper early Thursday. The 80-story tower houses Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, the sovereign wealth fund chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and central to his plans to diversify the economy beyond oil.
Three sources told Reuters an incoming Houthi missile hit the tower. The Saudi-led coalition said falling debris caused damage in Riyadh and gave no location. The Houthis have yet to claim responsibility, but there were no immediate reports of casualties.
It was the second attack to damage a major building in Riyadh’s financial district in less than two weeks. A November 8 attack damaged an office used by state oil giant Saudi Aramco. Houthi attacks on Saudi airports and oil infrastructure have intensified since fighting in Yemen resumed this summer.
